facts: Neutron stars are so unimaginably dense that a single teaspoon of their material weighs about 6 billion tons—roughly the weight of Mount Everest.
Time passes faster the higher you are from Earth's gravity; astronauts on the International Space Station age slightly faster than people on the ground.
There is a giant cloud of alcohol drifting in Sagittarius B2 containing enough ethyl alcohol to fill 400 trillion trillion pints of beer.
If two pieces of the same type of metal touch in the vacuum of space, they will permanently fuse together in a process known as 'cold welding'.

Saturn's moon Titan has liquid methane and ethane rain, rivers, and lakes, and its atmospheric pressure is dense enough that humans could walk around without a pressurized suit (though you'd still need an oxygen mask).
Light from the Sun takes roughly 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning if the Sun suddenly vanished, we wouldn't know about it until it went dark over 8 minutes later.
Because of how light travels across vast cosmic distances, when we look deep into space, we are literally looking back in time.
There are more trees on Earth—roughly 3 trillion—than there are stars in our Milky Way galaxy, which is estimated to be between 100 and 400 billion.
Venus spins backward compared to most other planets in our solar system, meaning the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east, and its day is longer than its year.
Space is completely silent because there is no air or medium for sound waves to travel through; sound cannot propagate in a vacuum.
The footprints left by the Apollo astronauts on the Moon will likely stay there for millions of years because there is no wind, water erosion, or atmosphere to erase them.
A year on Mercury is just 88 Earth days long, but a single solar day (from sunrise to sunrise) takes 176 Earth days, meaning its day is twice as long as its year.
Jupiter has a powerful magnetic field 20,000 times stronger than Earth's, creating a radiation belt so intense it can fry spacecraft electronics.
There is a rogue planet wandering through space called PSO J318.5-22 that floats completely free without orbiting a star, drifting 80 light-years away from Earth.
On Mars, sunsets do not glow red or orange like they do on Earth; instead, the fine dust particles in the Martian atmosphere scatter light to create an eerie blue sunset.
The largest known star in the universe, UY Scuti, is a hypergiant so massive that if it replaced our Sun, its outer surface would extend out past the orbit of Jupiter.
Comets are often described as 'dirty snowballs' because they are made of frozen gases, rock, and dust left over from the formation of the solar system 4.6 billion years ago.
If you tried to cry in space, your tears wouldn't fall down your face; instead, they would pool together into a stinging liquid blob that sticks to your skin due to surface tension.
The center of our Milky Way galaxy smells faintly of rum and tastes like raspberries, thanks to a massive cosmic cloud of ethyl formate floating in Sagittarius B2.
Pluto's heart-shaped glacier, known as Sputnik Planitia, is a massive basin of nitrogen ice that actively moves, melts, and reforms like a glacier on Earth.
A full NASA space suit is essentially a miniature spacecraft that costs around $12 million to build, with over 70% of that cost going toward the backpack life support system.
In 1977, humanity received a mysterious 72-second radio signal from deep space known as the 'Wow! Signal,' and astronomers still do not know for certain what caused it.
The colossal Olympus Mons on Mars is a shield volcano three times taller than Mount Everest, standing so high that its peak reaches completely out of the Martian atmosphere.
Due to space radiation and weightlessness, astronauts can grow up to 2 inches taller while living on the International Space Station, though they shrink back down upon returning to Earth.

Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners that suck everything up; if our Sun were replaced by a black hole of the exact same mass, Earth's orbit wouldn't change at all—we would just freeze in the dark.
The Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977, is the furthest human-made object in existence, currently traveling through interstellar space billions of miles away from Earth.
Astronomers have discovered a planet named WASP-12b that is so close to its parent star that tidal forces are stretching it into an egg shape, and the planet is being devoured alive.
The universe has no center; wherever you stand in the cosmos, every distant galaxy appears to be moving away from you, as the fabric of space itself is expanding.
Our Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth at a rate of about 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) every year because of tidal friction.
There is a diamond planet known as 55 Cancri e located 40 light-years away from Earth, where immense carbon pressure has crystallized a large portion of its internal structure into diamond.
Sunspots are dark patches on the Sun that appear black only by comparison to the surrounding bright gas; if you could isolate a sunspot, it would shine brighter than an electric arc lamp.
The Andromeda Galaxy is hurtling toward our Milky Way galaxy at a speed of about 250,000 miles per hour, and the two galaxies are projected to collide in about 4.5 billion years.
Saturn's density is so low that if you could find a bathtub big enough to hold it, the planet would float on water.
Neutron star collisions are responsible for forging massive amounts of heavy elements in the universe, including nearly all the gold and platinum found on Earth.
Astronauts on the International Space Station witness 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day because the station orbits Earth once every 90 minutes.

The coldest known place in the natural universe is the Boomerang Nebula, where temperatures drop down to minus 458 degrees Fahrenheit (-272 degrees Celsius), colder than the background radiation of space itself.
There are billions of rogue planets wandering the Milky Way completely untethered to any star system, meaning they exist in eternal, pitch-black night.
The magnetic field of a magnetar—a specialized type of neutron star—is so intense that if you got within 1,000 miles of it, the iron in the blood inside your body would literally distort.
The Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula are massive columns of cold interstellar hydrogen gas and dust, yet they are so vast that light takes several years just to cross them.

If two identical black holes merge together, the violent collision releases an unimaginable burst of energy in gravitational waves that momentarily outshines all the stars in the observable universe combined.
Spacecraft flying past Jupiter must endure intense radiation bands that generate a constant, high-pitched static noise capable of destroying unshielded microchips.
The largest asteroid in our solar system, Ceres, contains so much water ice that its mantle may hold more fresh water than all of Earth's oceans combined.

Because light takes time to travel, when we look at distant stars like Betelgeuse, we are seeing them as they looked centuries ago, and the star may have already exploded into a supernova without us knowing yet.
The Sun accounts for a staggering 99.86% of the total mass of our entire solar system, leaving just 0.14% for all the planets, moons, asteroids, and comets combined.
Saturn's tiny moon Enceladus shoots massive geysers of water ice and organic compounds from a subsurface ocean out into space, creating Saturn's faint E-ring.

The surface temperature of Mercury swings wildly from a scorching 800 degrees Fahrenheit (430 degrees Celsius) on its sunlit side to a freezing minus 290 degrees Fahrenheit (-180 degrees Celsius) on its dark side.
Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are mysterious, highly energetic flashes of cosmic radio waves that last mere milliseconds yet emit as much energy as the Sun produces in an entire century.
The constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear) is home to the Pinwheel Galaxy, a stunning cosmic pinwheel containing over a trillion stars spread across 170,000 light-years.
If you traveled at the speed of light, it would still take you over 100,000 years just to cross from one side of our Milky Way galaxy to the other.
The Hubble Space Telescope travels at a blistering speed of 17,500 miles per hour, orbiting Earth every 95 minutes while capturing razor-sharp images of deep space.
There is a colossal supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy named Sagittarius A* that weighs roughly 4 million times the mass of our Sun.
Mars has a massive canyon system called Valles Marineris that is so long it would stretch all the way from New York City to Los Angeles if placed across the United States.
The star system Gliese 665 contains red dwarf stars that burn their nuclear fuel so slowly they could theoretically live for trillions of years—longer than the current age of the universe.
The first living mammal sent into orbit was a stray dog from the streets of Moscow named Laika, launched aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957.
Cosmic microwave background radiation is the oldest light in the universe, representing the fading afterglow of the Big Bang that can still be detected as static on old analog television sets.
Uranus is the only planet in our solar system that rotates completely on its side, rolling along its orbital path like a barrel due to a massive ancient collision.
The universe contains at least two trillion individual galaxies, each harboring billions or even trillions of stars and planets.
Astronauts cannot burp in microgravity because without gravity separating liquids and gases in the stomach, burping turns into an unwanted wet bubble of stomach acid.
The largest volcano known in the solar system, Olympus Mons, has such a gentle slope that if you stood on its outer edge, the peak would be completely below the horizon.
Quasars are the brightest objects in the universe, powered by supermassive black holes consuming surrounding matter so fiercely they outshine entire galaxies.
The Sun loses roughly 4 million tons of mass every single second just by converting matter into pure energy through nuclear fusion.
There is a gigantic cloud of water vapor floating in deep space surrounding a quasar 12 billion light-years away, containing 140 trillion times more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.
Neptune's winds are the fastest in the solar system, whipping around the planet at supersonic speeds exceeding 1,200 miles per hour.

The James Webb Space Telescope is positioned nearly a million miles away from Earth at the Lagrange Point 2, where it uses a tennis-court-sized sunshield to keep its infrared sensors at freezing temperatures.
Neutron stars spin with terrifying speed; some pulsars rotate hundreds of times every single second like a cosmic lighthouse flashing beams of radiation.
The Moon has moonquakes caused by gravitational tidal forces from Earth, which can cause the lunar ground to rumble for hours at a time.

If you were pulled into a black hole feet-first, the extreme gravitational gradient would stretch your body lengthwise like a strand of spaghetti in a process astrophysicists call 'spaghettification'.
The Voyager Golden Records—golden phonograph records containing sounds and images selected to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth—are meant to last for a billion years.
Ganymede, the largest moon of Jupiter, is bigger than the planet Mercury and possesses its own internally generated magnetic field.
Space debris is becoming a growing hazard in low Earth orbit, where tiny paint flecks traveling at orbital speeds can shatter spacecraft windows upon impact.

The universe is roughly 13.8 billion years old, yet the light from the most distant galaxy discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope shows it as it existed just 300 million years after the Big Bang.
Saturn's rings are remarkably thin; despite being hundreds of thousands of miles wide, they are generally only about 30 feet thick.
The star Sirius, the brightest star in our night sky, is actually a binary star system consisting of a bright blue main-sequence star and a dense white dwarf companion.

In 1999, an asteroid named 1999 RQ36 (later named Bennu) was identified as having a small statistical chance of impacting Earth in the late 22nd century, prompting the OSIRIS-REx sample-return mission.
The temperature inside the core of the Sun reaches an astonishing 27 million degrees Fahrenheit (15 million degrees Celsius).
Comet Hale-Bopp, which lit up Earth's night sky in 1997, was so bright it could be seen with the naked eye even through light-polluted city skies for over 18 months.
The Oort Cloud, a distant shell of icy planetesimals surrounding our solar system, marks the absolute outer boundary of the Sun's gravitational influence.
Because of gravitational lensing predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity, massive galaxy clusters can bend and warp light from behind them like a giant cosmic magnifying glass.
The international space station travels fast enough to circle the entire planet Earth roughly 15.5 times every 24 hours.
There are mountains on Pluto made entirely of solid water ice that tower up to 3.5 kilometers high, floating on a sluggish glacier of nitrogen ice.
The largest known structure in the universe is the Hercules-Corona Borealis Great Wall, a gargantuan cosmic web of galaxy clusters spanning an unbelievable 10 billion light-years across.
Astronauts' sense of taste changes in space because bodily fluids shift upward toward the head due to microgravity, causing nasal congestion similar to having a bad cold.
The sun is classified as a yellow dwarf star, which means it is middle-aged and will spend another 5 billion years steadily fusing hydrogen into helium.
Io, the innermost Galilean moon of Jupiter, is the most volcanically active body in the entire solar system, featuring hundreds of sulfur volcanoes spewing plumes dozens of miles high.
The phrase 'the cosmos is within us' is scientifically literal: almost every element heavier than hydrogen and helium in our bodies was forged inside the fiery cores of dying stars.
There is a stellar nursery called the Carina Nebula where brilliant radiation from massive newborn stars is carving out pillars of dust and triggering waves of new star formation.
The Hubble Ultra Deep Field image captured light from over 10,000 distinct galaxies in a tiny, seemingly empty patch of sky no larger than a grain of sand held at arm's length.
White dwarfs are the leftover glowing carbon-oxygen cores of dead sun-like stars, packing a mass similar to our Sun into a sphere roughly the size of Earth.
The star Betelgeuse is so massive that if it sat at the center of our solar system, its outer edges would swallow up Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and possibly Jupiter.
The atmosphere of Jupiter features a colossal spinning storm known as the Great Red Spot, which is wide enough to swallow Earth whole and has been raging for over 300 years.
If two astronauts in space were to take off their helmets and float face-to-face in a vacuum, they would not explode, but they would lose consciousness within 15 seconds due to a lack of oxygen.
The first artificial satellite to orbit Earth was Sputnik 1, launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957, initiating the global space age.
The interstellar medium—the space between star systems—is not a pure vacuum; it contains about one atom of gas per cubic centimeter along with microscopic dust grains.
The largest known impact crater on Mars, the Hellas Planitia basin, spans over 1,300 miles across and is deep enough to bury Mount Everest.
Supernovae are so intensely energetic that a single exploding star can temporarily outshine an entire galaxy composed of billions of stars.
The planet Uranus was originally named 'Georgium Sidus' (George's Star) by its discoverer William Herschel in honor of King George III.
Dark matter makes up roughly 27% of the total mass-energy content of the universe, yet scientists still have never directly detected a single particle of it.
Dark energy accounts for about 68% of the universe and is driving the accelerated expansion of the cosmos, forcing distant galaxies apart at unimaginable speeds.
The Parker Solar Probe touches the Sun's atmosphere, flying closer to our star than any spacecraft in history while enduring blistering temperatures over 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit.
The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second, acting as the absolute cosmic speed limit for everything in the universe.
The moon Titan has a dense, nitrogen-rich atmosphere thicker than Earth's, complete with organic haze layers and weather cycles involving liquid methane.
Neutron stars possess gravitational fields so intense that light passing close to them gets severely bent and distorted in a phenomenon called gravitational deflection.
The galaxy GN-z11 is one of the oldest and most distant galaxies ever observed, seen as it existed just 400 million years after the Big Bang.
Spacecraft navigating interplanetary journeys must account for gravitational assists, stealing momentum from planets like Jupiter or Venus to slingshot themselves deeper into the solar system.
The center of the Andromeda Galaxy contains a double nucleus featuring a dense cluster of stars whipping around a supermassive black hole at breakneck speeds.
Astronauts wear diapers during rocket launches and spacewalks because getting out of a multi-million-dollar space suit to use a restroom is virtually impossible.
The term 'light-year' is a measure of distance, not time—it represents the staggering distance that a beam of light travels in one Earth year, roughly 5.88 trillion miles.
There is a curious cosmic phenomenon called spaghettification where intense tidal forces near black holes stretch objects horizontally and vertically.
The rings of Uranus are pitch black and composed of extremely dark methane-ice chunks, making them notoriously difficult to detect without specialized infrared telescopes.
The largest canyon on Venus, Diana Chasma, plunges nearly 4 miles deep into the planet's scorching, volcanic crust.
The star Eta Carinae is an unstable hypergiant system that is expected to explode in a cataclysmic supernova sometime in the astronomically near future.
Astronauts working outside the International Space Station wear tethered safety lines because drifting away into open space without propulsion would mean certain death.
The first human being to journey into outer space was Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, who successfully orbited Earth aboard Vostok 1 on April 12, 1961.
Comet McNaught lit up the southern hemisphere in 2007 with a tail so brilliant and massive that it could be easily seen in broad daylight.
The solar wind is a continuous stream of charged particles ejected from the upper atmosphere of the Sun, bathing the entire solar system in high-energy plasma.
The aurora borealis and australis (Northern and Southern lights) are caused when charged solar wind particles collide with gas molecules in Earth's upper atmosphere.
The planet Saturn has 146 officially recognized moons, making it the planet with the most natural satellites in our solar system.
The density of a black hole's singularity is theoretically infinite, compressing a massive amount of matter down into a geometric point of zero volume.
The interstellar object 'Oumuamua was the first known interstellar visitor to pass through our solar system, baffling scientists with its unusual elongated shape and non-gravitational acceleration.
The cosmic web is a vast, skeletal network of filaments composed of dark matter and galaxies that spans across the entire observable universe.
The largest known star cluster, R136a1, contains monster stars over 200 times more massive than our Sun, blazing with an intense blue-white ultraviolet glow.
The first woman to travel into space was Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova, who orbited Earth 48 times during her solo mission in 1963.
The surface of Venus is hot enough to melt lead, with ambient temperatures hovering around 900 degrees Fahrenheit (475 degrees Celsius) day and night.
If you could compress all the empty space out of the atoms making up every human being on Earth, the entire global population would fit inside the volume of a single sugar cube.
The star Polaris has served as the North Star for navigators for centuries, though due to Earth's axial wobble, other stars like Vega will take its place in the distant future.
The coldest temperature ever recorded in the laboratory is a fraction of a billionth of a degree above absolute zero, far colder than any naturally occurring region in deep space.
The massive impact basin known as the South Pole-Aitken on the Moon's far side is one of the largest impact craters in the solar system, spanning over 1,500 miles.
The phrase 'the heavens declare the glory of God' has inspired astronomers for centuries, merging deep spiritual awe with mathematical precision.

The Voyager 1 spacecraft carries a copper phonograph record encoded with greetings in 55 languages, animal sounds, music ranging from Bach to Chuck Berry, and cultural instructions for any extraterrestrial intelligence that might find it.
The largest known galaxy IC 1101 is a behemoth elliptical galaxy spanning over 6 million light-years across, big enough to swallow our Milky Way and Andromeda combined several times over.
Space dust coats everything on the Moon, and Apollo astronauts discovered that abrasive lunar dust smells remarkably like spent gunpowder after being tracked inside their lunar modules.
The rings of Neptune are so faint and patchy that they were completely missed by early telescopic sweeps until Voyager 2 flew past in 1989.
The star Vega was the very first star other than our Sun to ever be photographed, captured via a daguerreotype process in July 1850.
The cosmic horizon defines the absolute boundary of our observable universe, sitting roughly 46.5 billion light-years away in all directions.
The planet Mars has two tiny, potato-shaped moons named Phobos and Deimos, which are widely believed to be captured asteroids from the nearby asteroid belt.
The first successful landing on the Moon was achieved by the Soviet unmanned probe Luna 2, which impacted the lunar surface in September 1959.
The Hubble Space Telescope's mirror was initially ground with a microscopic flaw the width of 1/50th of a human hair, which made its early images blurry until corrective optics were installed.
The magnetic poles of Earth periodically flip completely, with the North and South magnetic poles swapping places over geological time scales.
The star cluster known as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters) is cradled within a reflection nebula that lights up as the hot young stars pass through interstellar dust.
The highest mountain peak in the solar system, Olympus Mons, has a base so massive that its entire footprint would cover the entire state of Arizona.
The first commercial space tourist to visit the International Space Station was American engineer Dennis Tito, who paid his own way aboard a Soyuz spacecraft in 2001.
The center of our galaxy contains a massive star cluster known as the Arches Cluster, packed with over a hundred searing, massive young stars.
The solar flare is a sudden flash of increased sun brightness, usually observed near its surface and close to a sunspot group, releasing immense radiation.
The speed of gravitational waves travels at exactly the speed of light, as confirmed by the simultaneous detection of light and gravitational ripples from a neutron star merger.
The planet Jupiter acts as a celestial vacuum cleaner, its immense gravity helping to shield inner planets like Earth from frequent catastrophic asteroid strikes.
The term 'astronaut' comes from Greek roots meaning 'star sailor', while the Russian equivalent 'cosmonaut' means 'universe sailor'.
The first animal to orbit Earth was a Soviet space dog named Laika, though she tragically survived only a few hours due to overheating.
The Great Attractor is a massive gravitational anomaly located tens of millions of light-years away, pulling our Milky Way galaxy and thousands of other galaxies toward it across the cosmos.
The surface of Mars experiences terrifying global dust storms that can envelop the entire planet for months, blocking out the Sun completely.
The first American woman to fly in space was Sally Ride, who blasted off aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger on June 18, 1983.
The star system Alpha Centauri is our closest stellar neighbor, located about 4.37 light-years away and consisting of three separate stars: Rigil Kentaurus, Toliman, and Proxima Centauri.
The coldest object ever detected in the universe outside of a laboratory is the Boomerang Nebula, where expanding gas cools down faster than deep space background radiation.
The rings of Saturn are composed of billions of individual particles ranging in size from tiny microscopic dust grains to massive mountain-sized chunks of water ice.
The first human footprint on the Moon was stepped by Neil Armstrong on July 20, 1969, during the historic Apollo 11 mission.
The concept of a black hole was first mathematically hypothesized by clergyman and geologist John Michell in 1783 using Isaac Newton's laws of gravitation.
The star Betelgeuse underwent an unprecedented 'Great Dimming' in late 2019 and early 2020, dropping significantly in brightness before recovering, caused by a massive surface dust eruption.
The universe's first stars were forged almost entirely out of pristine hydrogen and helium, completely devoid of heavy elements like carbon or iron.
The largest known diamond in the universe is a white dwarf star named BPM 37093, nicknamed 'Lucy' after the Beatles song, featuring a crystalline carbon core 2,500 miles across.
The planet Saturn's hexagonal storm at its north pole is a massive, persistent six-sided cloud pattern wider than two Earths combined.
The phrase 'Houston, we have a problem' is a famous misquote from Apollo 13; the actual transmission spoken by astronaut Jack Swigert was: 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.'
The cosmic dust floating through space contains complex organic carbon compounds, suggesting that the chemical building blocks of life are widespread across the galaxy.
The largest known ring system in the universe belongs to the giant star J1407b, whose rings are nearly 200 times larger than Saturn's and would dominate our night sky if placed in our solar system.
The atmospheric pressure on the surface of Venus is 92 times that of Earth, equivalent to the pressure experienced nearly a kilometer underwater in Earth's oceans.
The star Polaris is not a single fixed point; it is a triple star system located roughly 433 light-years away from Earth.
The Milky Way galaxy is warped and twisted at its edges like a potato chip, distorted by the gravitational pull of passing satellite dwarf galaxies.
The first spacecraft to successfully land on Mars and transmit surface images back to Earth was Viking 1 in July 1976.
The energy output of a single gamma-ray burst—the most luminous electromagnetic events in the universe—can exceed the total energy output of our Sun over its entire 10-billion-year lifespan.
The planet Mercury has virtually no atmosphere to trap heat, which is why its temperature plummets to bone-chilling lows on its night side despite its proximity to the Sun.
The concept of the Big Bang was initially ridiculed by physicist Fred Hoyle, who coined the term derisively during a BBC radio broadcast in 1949.
The International Space Station orbits Earth at an altitude of roughly 250 miles, crossing paths with orbital debris that occasionally requires emergency collision avoidance maneuvers.
The constellation Orion contains the Orion Nebula, a sprawling stellar nursery visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy patch of light in Orion's sword.
The moon Io has sulfur lava lakes and geysers that shoot volcanic plumes up to 300 miles high into the thin vacuum of space.
The first photograph of a black hole's shadow was captured in 2019 by the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration, imaging the supermassive black hole at the center of galaxy M87.
The distance from Earth to the Sun defines an astronomical unit (AU), which equals approximately 93 million miles (150 million kilometers).
The planet Jupiter features a faint, wispy ring system discovered by Voyager 1 that is composed primarily of microscopic dust blasted off its small inner moons.
The star system TRAPPIST-1 boasts seven rocky Earth-sized planets orbiting a tiny ultracool dwarf star, with three of them sitting comfortably in the habitable zone.
The speed of sound varies depending on the medium; while sound travels at about 767 mph in Earth's air, it travels much faster through water and dense solid materials.
The first operational space station was the Soviet Salyut 1, launched into low Earth orbit in April 1971.
The massive dark patches visible on the Moon's surface are called maria (Latin for 'seas'), which are actually ancient plains of solidified basaltic lava flows.
The universe contains roughly ten times more stars than all the grains of sand on every beach and desert on planet Earth combined.
The star Arcturus is a bright red giant that is currently moving through space so fast it crosses an area of the sky equivalent to the Moon's width every 800 years.
The planet Saturn's moon Titan is the only moon in the solar system with a dense atmosphere and stable bodies of liquid on its surface.
The term 'supernova' was first popularized by astrophysicists Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s to describe exceptionally bright stellar explosions.
The first live television broadcast from space was transmitted by American astronauts during the historic Apollo 11 moon mission in 1969.
The universe's expansion is not slowing down; observations of distant supernovae reveal that the expansion is actually speeding up due to mysterious dark energy.
The star Rigel in the constellation Orion is a blue supergiant star that shines with the luminosity of roughly 120,000 suns.
The planet Mars has polar ice caps composed of a mixture of water ice and frozen carbon dioxide (dry ice) that expand and shrink with the Martian seasons.
The first woman to command the International Space Station was NASA astronaut Peggy Whitson, who broke numerous records for cumulative time spent in space.
The universe is remarkably flat on large scales, meaning parallel beams of light will theoretically travel parallel forever without converging or diverging.
The star system Castor in the constellation Gemini is a complex sextuple star system consisting of six individual stars orbiting a common center of mass.
The planet Venus rotates so slowly that its metallic core fails to generate a significant planetary magnetic field, leaving it vulnerable to solar wind erosion.
The first successful interplanetary flyby was achieved by NASA's Mariner 2 probe, which passed by Venus in December 1962.
The universe's oldest known star, informally named the 'Methuselah star' (HD 140283), is estimated to be nearly as old as the universe itself.
The constellation Scorpius contains the bright red supergiant star Antares, which is so massive that if placed in our solar system, its edge would reach past the orbit of Mars.
The planet Mercury experiences a strange orbital resonance where it rotates three times on its axis for every two times it orbits the Sun.
The first animal to successfully return alive from space orbit was a pair of Soviet dogs named Belka and Strelka, along with a rabbit and 42 mice, in August 1960.
The universe contains immense cosmic magnetic fields permeating interstellar and intergalactic space, though their exact origin remains a mystery to modern physics.
The star system Procyon is a bright binary star system located in the constellation Canis Minor, featuring a yellow-white main-sequence star and a faint white dwarf.
The planet Jupiter's Great Red Spot has been shrinking over the past century, baffling meteorologists and planetary scientists studying its storm dynamics.
The first successful lunar landing of a reusable robotic rover was accomplished by the Soviet Lunokhod 1 in November 1970.
The universe's background radiation hums with a faint microwave glow that represents the oldest electromagnetic footprint in existence.
The star system Polaris is used by navigators in the Northern Hemisphere because it sits almost directly above Earth's geographic North Pole.
The planet Mars features towering dust devils that can rise miles high into the thin Martian atmosphere, kicking up dark trails across desert plains.
The first American to orbit Earth was John Glenn, who completed three orbits aboard the Friendship 7 capsule on February 20, 1962.
The universe's structural distribution of galaxies resembles a giant cosmic sponge, featuring vast empty voids surrounded by dense intersecting filaments of dark matter.
The star system Sirius is slowly drifting closer to our solar system, meaning it will appear slightly brighter in Earth's night sky over the next 60,000 years.
The planet Saturn's moon Mimas features a gigantic impact crater named Herschel that gives the tiny moon an uncanny resemblance to the Death Star from Star Wars.
The first successful deep-space probe to photograph the outer gas giants up close was NASA's Pioneer 10 in the early 1970s.

The planet Uranus was discovered accidentally by astronomer William Herschel with a telescope from his garden in Bath, England, in March 1781.
The first human-made object to crash into the Moon was the Soviet Luna 2 probe in September 1959.
The universe's most distant detected individual star, Earendel, existed when the cosmos was just 900 million years old, its light magnified by a massive galaxy cluster acting as a gravitational lens.
The star system Alpha Centauri is often considered humanity's most logical first destination for future interstellar robotic exploration probes.
The planet Neptune was discovered through mathematical calculations based on irregularities in Uranus's orbit before astronomers actually spotted it through a telescope.
The first successful soft landing on Venus was achieved by the Soviet Venera 7 probe in December 1970, transmitting data from the scorching surface for 23 minutes before succumbing to extreme heat.
The universe's elemental composition is overwhelmingly dominated by hydrogen and helium, which account for over 98% of all ordinary matter.
The star system Betelgeuse experiences rhythmic pulsations that cause its physical size to expand and contract by millions of miles over regular cycles.
The planet Mars has a thin carbon dioxide atmosphere that offers almost no protection against harsh solar and cosmic radiation.
The first successful photograph of Earth from lunar orbit was captured by NASA's Lunar Orbiter 1 in August 1966.
The universe's supermassive black holes grow in tandem with their host galaxies, suggesting a deep, mysterious evolutionary link between galaxy formation and black hole growth.
The star system Rigel is part of a quadruple star system, though its smaller companion stars are difficult to resolve without powerful telescopes.
The planet Jupiter's internal pressure is so immense that it liquefies hydrogen into a vast metallic ocean that generates the planet's powerful magnetic field.
The first successful soft landing on Mars was achieved by NASA's Viking 1 lander in July 1976.
The universe's ultimate fate remains an open scientific question, with theories ranging from endless expansion and heat death to a potential future cosmic contraction.
The star system Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus appears red to the naked eye because it is an aging red giant star burning through its final fuel reserves.
The planet Saturn's density is so low that if an ocean could be found large enough, the giant ringed planet would bob like a basketball in water.
The first human to spend more than a year continuously in space was Soviet cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov aboard the Mir space station.
The universe's first complex molecules, such as hydride ions, formed in space hundreds of millions of years after the Big Bang, paving the way for chemistry across the cosmos.
